### Problem: Boats to Save People {#sec-tp-p4-a}

::: {.p-statement}
Weights $p_0, \dots, p_{n-1}$ ($1 \le n \le 5\cdot10^4$, $1 \le p_i \le \mathit{limit} \le 3\cdot10^4$). Each boat carries **at most two** people and their total weight must be $\le \mathit{limit}$. Every person boards. Return the **minimum number of boats**.

Source: [LC 881 · Boats to Save People](https://leetcode.com/problems/boats-to-save-people/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Each boat holds one or two people and everyone must board, so the number of boats is $n$ minus the number of shared boats: minimising boats is maximising *pairs*. Sort, then look at the heaviest person still waiting: they must ride, and the only person worth pairing them with is the **lightest** waiting one — if even the lightest is too heavy to share, the heaviest goes alone and *no* partner could have helped. This "test heaviest with lightest" is the opposite-ends walk of @sec-tp-p1 with a new rule: the heaviest finger moves every step, the lightest only when it found a seat.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Exact minimum via maximum pairing.** A boat count equals $n - (\text{max disjoint valid pairs})$. Compute the max pairing by bitmask DP over small $n$. Exponential — oracle only.
2. **Sort, pair the ends.** $\mathit{lo}=0$, $\mathit{hi}=n-1$; if $p[\mathit{lo}] + p[\mathit{hi}] \le \mathit{limit}$ pair them ($\mathit{lo}{+}{+}$), else the heaviest rides alone; always $\mathit{hi}{-}{-}$ and count one boat. $O(n\log n)$.

**Invariant.** After each step the heaviest person $p[\mathit{hi}]$ is committed to a boat, and the decision (shared with $p[\mathit{lo}]$ or alone) is optimal for that person, so the remaining subproblem is independent — the classic greedy exchange argument.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Exact pairing (bitmask DP)

::: {.form-next}
Turn "fewest boats" into "most two-person trips that fit" and solve it exactly with a mask DP: pick the lowest-index unbussed person, try leaving them solo or pairing them with any compatible unbussed person. $O(2^n \cdot n)$ — a checker, not a contest solution.

**Bitmask DP, in plain words (why this is only an oracle).** A *bitmask* is an integer whose binary digits mark which people are already seated — bit $i$ set means person $i$ has a boat. The recursion looks at the first still-unseated person and branches two ways: put them in alone, or pair them with each compatible unseated person. `@lru_cache` remembers results already computed for a given mask so we don't redo them. Boats needed $= n - (\text{maximum number of valid pairs})$, since each pair saves exactly one boat. It explores $2^n$ masks, so it is only usable as a checker for tiny $n$.

**Worked example.** people $= [3, 2, 2, 1]$, limit $= 3$. The only pair that fits is $1 + 2 = 3$, so at most one disjoint pair exists; boats $= 4 - 1 = 3$.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def num_boats_brute(people, limit):        # people passed as a tuple
    n = len(people)
    @lru_cache(None)
    def maxpairs(mask):
        first = next((i for i in range(n) if not (mask >> i) & 1), None)
        if first is None:
            return 0
        best = maxpairs(mask | (1 << first))               # first rides solo
        for j in range(first + 1, n):
            if not (mask >> j) & 1 and people[first] + people[j] <= limit:
                best = max(best, 1 + maxpairs(mask | (1 << first) | (1 << j)))
        return best
    return n - maxpairs(0)
```

##### C++

```cpp
// fragment - exact exponential baseline (small n only)
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
int boatsBrute(vector<int> p, int limit) {
    sort(p.begin(), p.end());
    int n = (int)p.size(), best = n + 1;
    function<void(int, int)> dfs = [&](int mask, int boats) {
        if (__builtin_popcount(mask) == n) { best = min(best, boats); return; }
        int a = -1; for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) if (!(mask >> i & 1)) { a = i; break; }
        dfs(mask | 1 << a, boats + 1);                    // a solo
        for (int b = a + 1; b < n; ++b)
            if (!(mask >> b & 1) && p[a] + p[b] <= limit)
                dfs(mask | 1 << a | 1 << b, boats + 1);
    };
    dfs(0, 0);
    return best;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `first = next(...)` finds the lowest-index person not yet in `mask` — always seating the smallest unhandled index so each grouping is generated once. `best = maxpairs(mask | (1 << first))` is the "first rides solo" branch; the loop then tries pairing `first` with every later unseated `j` that fits (`people[first] + people[j] <= limit`), taking `1 +` a pair over the solo option. `@lru_cache` memoises by mask so the $2^n$ states are each solved once. `n - maxpairs(0)` converts the maximum-pair count into the minimum boat count.

#### Sort, pair the ends

::: {.form-next}
The greedy. Sort once, then a two-pointer squeeze: give the heaviest waiting person the lightest waiting partner when they fit, else let the heaviest go alone. Each step settles one boat and consumes the heaviest, so it is $O(n)$ after the sort. The proof is the exchange: pairing the heaviest with anyone *heavier than the lightest* can only waste room.

**The greedy, in plain words.** Sort so weight increases left-to-right. The heaviest waiting person ($p[\mathit{hi}]$) *must* board some boat; the cheapest way to fill their spare capacity is with the *lightest* waiting person ($p[\mathit{lo}]$). If even the lightest is too heavy to share, then nobody can, so the heaviest goes alone. Either way the heaviest is settled, so we always move $\mathit{hi}$ in and count one boat. Why the lightest is the right partner is an *exchange argument* (@sec-pf-p3): in any optimal plan where the heaviest $H$ shares with someone else or rides alone, swapping the lightest $L$ into $H$'s boat keeps every boat legal and does not add a boat. Exercise 10 of the chapter writes the swap out in full.

**Worked example.** people $= [3, 2, 2, 1]$, limit $= 3$, sorted $= [1, 2, 2, 3]$. $\mathit{lo}=0(1)+\mathit{hi}=3(3)=4>3$ → heaviest alone, boat 1, $\mathit{hi}\to2$. $1+2=3\le3$ → pair them, $\mathit{lo}\to1$, $\mathit{hi}\to1$, boat 2. Now $\mathit{lo}=\mathit{hi}=1$: a single person left, they ride alone, boat 3. Answer $3$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("boats", "greedy")
    assert str(final) == "3"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-boats-people
def num_boats(people, limit):
    people = sorted(people)
    lo, hi, boats = 0, len(people) - 1, 0
    while lo <= hi:
        if people[lo] + people[hi] <= limit:
            lo += 1                 # lightest can share with heaviest
        hi -= 1                     # heaviest is committed either way
        boats += 1
    return boats

for _ in range(300):
    people = [random.randint(1, limit_ := 8) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 8))]
    assert num_boats(people, limit_) == num_boats_brute(tuple(people), limit_)
assert num_boats([1, 2], 3) == 1
assert num_boats([3, 2, 2, 1], 3) == 3            # the board sample
assert num_boats([3, 5, 3, 4], 5) == 4
print("num_boats OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

int numBoats(vector<int> people, int limit) {
    sort(people.begin(), people.end());
    int lo = 0, hi = (int)people.size() - 1, boats = 0;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        if (people[lo] + people[hi] <= limit) ++lo;
        --hi; ++boats;
    }
    return boats;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `people = sorted(people)` is what lets "heaviest" and "lightest" mean the two array ends. `lo, hi, boats = 0, len(people)-1, 0` sets up the squeeze and a counter. `while lo <= hi` (inclusive, so one leftover person at $\mathit{lo}=\mathit{hi}$ is still boarded). `if people[lo] + people[hi] <= limit: lo += 1` pairs the lightest with the heaviest when they fit; crucially `hi -= 1` and `boats += 1` run **unconditionally**, because the heaviest person is committed to a boat whether they shared it or rode alone — that is why a solo rider never causes an infinite loop.

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Exact pairing** is $O(2^n n)$ time and space — a stress oracle for $n \lesssim 18$. **Sort, pair the ends** is $O(n\log n)$ time, dominated by the sort, and $O(1)$ extra space (or $O(n)$ for Python's `sorted`). The greedy is the standard "fewest groups of at most two under a capacity" template. @sec-tp-p4-b keeps the sorted ends but drops the capacity: everyone is paired and the *largest* pair sum is minimised.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- A person heavier than $\mathit{limit} - \min p$ can never share: the `<= limit` test sends them alone and the loop still commits them via `hi -= 1`, so `lo <= hi` terminates cleanly (never an infinite loop on a solo rider).
- Everyone at most $\mathit{limit}/2$: every two fit, so boats $= \lceil n/2 \rceil$. Everyone above $\mathit{limit}/2$: nobody can share, so boats $= n$.
- `while lo < hi` is the classic bug: it never boards the last person when the fingers meet, and $[1, 2, 3]$ with $\mathit{limit} = 3$ returns $1$ instead of $2$.
- $n = 1$: one boat.
:::
